description: How the organization decides what to do next, and when to stop deciding and ask a human. The declarative workflow says what must be true; this says how the system converges on it when reality does not match the plan.
why: A workflow that only describes the happy path leaves the interesting question unanswered: what happens when a review rejects, a test keeps failing, or the architecture turns out to be wrong. Without an answer the system either retries forever or stops dead.
Every loop here is bounded. An unbounded retry is indistinguishable from a hang, and the third identical failure is information about the plan rather than about the attempt.

implement.why: Three rounds of the same rework means the acceptance criteria, the design, or an unwritten disagreement is the problem. A fourth round hides that instead of surfacing it.

diagnose.why: Replanning twice on the same work item means the problem was not understood at intake. A third replan is a new work item, not a better plan.

verify.why: Verification that keeps failing on the same evidence is not flaky; it is correct.

decide.description: Given an observed task outcome, what the loop does next. Evaluated top to bottom; the first match wins.

rules.why: The bound exists to be honoured. Checked before retry so an exhausted task cannot loop once more.
The same failure twice, by class and signature rather than by wording. A different failure each time is progress; this is not, and a third attempt only spends tokens to learn what is already known.
A rejection is information the implementer has not seen yet.
The graph is no longer a description of the work.
Evidence beat the design. Continuing would build on something known to be wrong.
An agent that guesses here produces work nobody can trust. A DEC is cheaper than the rework.
Not a failure. The organization is waiting on a human, and the liveness policy decides when that wait becomes a problem.
Only after every rule above has declined it. Retry is the last resort, not the first instinct.

triggers: dependency conflict that reordering cannot resolve
test evidence contradicts a stated assumption
a security finding changes what may be built
an API or schema contract conflict between parallel tasks
implementation complexity materially exceeds the plan
an external system the plan depended on is unavailable
requires: The diagnosis is written down before the new plan is generated. A replan with no recorded reason is indistinguishable from thrashing.
The superseded generation stays in history.jsonl. What the organization used to believe is evidence about how it plans.
Tasks already accepted are carried forward rather than redone, unless the diagnosis says their result is invalid.
replan.on_exhaustion: escalate to the human owner: two replans means the intake was wrong

escalation.record: Every escalation appends to the work item's history with the trigger, the evidence and the target. An escalation nobody recorded is a decision nobody can review.

mechanical: scripts/control_loop.py refuses to hand out a task whose attempts are exhausted
scripts/control_loop.py refuses to replan past max_per_work_item
hooks/scripts/observe_subagent.py records every subagent result against its task
advisory: Which decide rule applies to an observed failure is a judgement the model makes. The bounds on retrying and replanning are not.

failure_identity.description: How the loop decides two failures are the same one. Comparing the raw text was wrong in both directions: 'API returns 401' and 'endpoint still returns 401' are one failure and read as two, while 'failed' twice reads as one and can be two unrelated causes.

fields.class: The kind of failure: test_failure, review_rejected, contract_conflict, missing_information, dependency_unavailable, timeout, permission_denied, environment, unknown.
fields.signature: A stable identity for THIS failure, not a description of it. Supplied by whoever observed it where possible, derived otherwise.
fields.evidence: Where to look: a test path, a log line, an artifact id.
fields.message: Prose for a human. Never compared.

derivation.why: An observer that has to invent a signature will not supply one, so the loop derives one when it is missing. Derivation is deliberately conservative: it keeps only tokens that identify a failure -- exception names, status codes, test paths, error identifiers -- and discards prose entirely.
derivation.on_no_tokens: no-signature, which never matches anything, including itself. Deciding two failures are the same on no evidence is worse than deciding they differ: a wrong 'same' escalates work that was making progress.

failure_identity.comparison: Same class AND same signature means the same failure. Class alone is too coarse -- two unrelated test failures are both test_failure -- and signature alone would collide across kinds.

lease.why: A task claimed by an agent that never stopped is held forever: runnable() skips a leased task, so one crashed session strands every task behind it and the graph looks busy while being finished. The concurrency ledger already expires its slots on the same reasoning -- a stuck slot is worse than a missed one -- and the task lease, which costs more when it sticks, had no such rule.
lease.on_expiry: The lease is dropped and the task becomes runnable again. Its attempts are unchanged, so a task that keeps being claimed and abandoned still reaches its cap and escalates rather than cycling.

acceptance.why: The four answers a definition of done can give are not equally serious, and how much each is allowed to hold up an acceptance is an organizational decision rather than a branch in Python. Stating it here means a project can tighten it.

failing.why: The repository can see it is not done. There is no risk level at which that is acceptable.

unsupported.why: The checker cannot answer, which is a broken contract rather than evidence elsewhere. Refusing every session over it would make the gate unusable; passing it silently makes the gate pointless.

unverifiable.why: Real evidence that lives in GitLab or a pipeline. Nothing in a session can confirm it, so refusing would block work on the platform's shape rather than on the work. Every acceptance names which predicates rested on it.
unverifiable.what_would_change_this: A project that can read its own pipeline results should set CRITICAL to refuse, because then the evidence is reachable and resting on an assertion is a choice.
